Edge-weight stability and split-half reliability

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland
Source: vignettes/articles/network-reliability.Rmd
network-reliability.Rmd

Can the strongest edges and most prominent nodes in a psychological network be trusted to remain similar in another sample? Consider a network of self-efficacy, learning strategies and test anxiety, in which the constructs are nodes and their estimated associations are edges. In a partial correlation network, each edge describes an association adjusted for the other variables, while centrality measures summarise aspects of each node’s position. These tools allow researchers to explore multivariate patterns rather than examine every construct in isolation (Borsboom et al., 2021). Yet the interpretation of edge weights and centrality depends on the estimation method and available data, making stability and reliability important considerations (Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2023).

Network methods have been used in education to study the relationships among learning processes and how these relationships vary across contexts and time. Saqr et al. (2024) introduce psychological networks as an approach to analysing learning and complex learning processes. Applications include networks of students’ monitoring events across phases of regulation (Malmberg et al., 2022) and the temporal dynamics of self-regulation during academic writing (Saqr et al., 2021). These studies illustrate the value of examining patterns of relationships, but an apparent connection or prominent node in an estimated network should not automatically be treated as a reproducible finding.

A network fitted to one sample will generally differ from a network fitted to another sample from the same population. Consequently, applied researchers need to assess uncertainty in individual edge weights, whether nodes can be distinguished in centrality, and how much the network changes when observations are omitted or divided into groups. Resampling provides an empirical way to investigate these questions by repeatedly estimating networks from the available observations (Epskamp et al., 2018). Assessing and clearly reporting such uncertainty is also part of good practice in cross-sectional network analysis (Burger et al., 2023). These checks describe the robustness of an estimated network; they do not establish causal relationships or guarantee replication in a new population.

This article demonstrates five complementary diagnostics in psychnets: bootstrap intervals for edges and centrality, bootstrap comparisons of nodes, case-dropping stability of centrality, case-dropping reliability of edge weights, and split-half reliability. The worked example uses questionnaire responses generated by a large language model, rather than observations of students, and therefore illustrates methods rather than substantive findings about learners. For each diagnostic, we explain the question it addresses, show the relevant output, and discuss what researchers can reasonably report. The functions use a consistent network-estimation interface, allowing the same workflow to be used with other estimators.

library(psychnets)
set.seed(1)

Because the procedures involve random resampling, setting the seed makes the illustrative results reproducible.

Data

SRL_Claude contains 300 sets of responses to the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire generated by the large language model Claude for a study of responses to psychological surveys (Vogelsmeier et al., 2025). The model-generated responses are unusually internally consistent and produce several large estimated edges. They make the numerical examples easy to inspect, but do not provide evidence about relationships among constructs in real students.

  • Nodes: five construct scores on a scale from 1 to 7: CSU (cognitive strategy use), IV (intrinsic value), SE (self-efficacy), SR (self-regulation) and TA (test anxiety).
  • Observations: one row per respondent; the data are complete.
head(SRL_Claude)
#>        CSU       IV       SE       SR   TA
#> 1 4.615385 6.444444 4.555556 4.777778 4.00
#> 2 5.692308 7.000000 5.555556 6.222222 3.00
#> 3 5.692308 7.000000 5.777778 6.666667 3.75
#> 4 5.461538 6.222222 5.777778 5.777778 4.75
#> 5 4.846154 5.333333 5.000000 5.333333 3.75
#> 6 4.538462 4.333333 5.777778 4.000000 5.00

The main analyses use an EBIC graphical lasso (method = "glasso") to estimate a regularised network of partial correlations. All five diagnostics therefore assess the same type of fitted network.

How precise is each edge?

net_boot() draws samples of observations with replacement, estimates a network for each sample and summarises the resulting edge weights. The output provides each observed weight, the bootstrap mean, a 95% percentile interval and the proportion of resamples in which the edge has a non-zero estimate. The significant flag indicates that the percentile interval excludes zero; it should not be read as proof of an underlying relationship. For substantive research, at least 1,000 bootstrap samples provide a more useful basis for assessing precision. Here, 200 resamples keep the demonstration manageable.

b <- net_boot(SRL_Claude, method = "glasso", n_boot = 200, cores = 1)
b
#> <psychnet_bootstrap> glasso, 200 resamples, 95% CI
#>   10 edges (8 significant), 5 nodes, measures: strength, expected_influence
as.data.frame(b)
#>    from to     observed        mean      lower      upper prop_nonzero
#> 1   CSU IV  0.001744267  0.02777141  0.0000000  0.1202986        0.550
#> 2   CSU SE  0.223973564  0.22825629  0.1360369  0.3243276        1.000
#> 3    IV SE -0.402239002 -0.40747351 -0.5171210 -0.2997294        1.000
#> 4   CSU SR  0.728177591  0.72069631  0.6520409  0.7748107        1.000
#> 5    IV SR  0.574170376  0.55984489  0.4974457  0.6284297        1.000
#> 6    SE SR  0.221496430  0.22481115  0.1522627  0.3150743        1.000
#> 7   CSU TA  0.525584044  0.52512504  0.4465139  0.6111719        1.000
#> 8    IV TA -0.013854928 -0.03375546 -0.1320652  0.0245725        0.755
#> 9    SE TA -0.417575459 -0.41986895 -0.4934429 -0.3408875        1.000
#> 10   SR TA -0.428181457 -0.42032870 -0.4852677 -0.3476119        1.000
#>    significant
#> 1        FALSE
#> 2         TRUE
#> 3         TRUE
#> 4         TRUE
#> 5         TRUE
#> 6         TRUE
#> 7         TRUE
#> 8        FALSE
#> 9         TRUE
#> 10        TRUE

Eight of the ten edges have percentile intervals that exclude zero, and all eight are selected in every bootstrap sample. The largest positive edge, CSU–SR, has an observed weight of 0.73 and an interval from 0.65 to 0.77. By contrast, CSU–IV has a weight of 0.002, an interval from 0 to 0.12 and a non-zero estimate in 55% of resamples. The IV–TA edge has a weight of -0.014, an interval from -0.13 to 0.02 and a non-zero estimate in 75.5% of resamples. The latter two intervals include zero, so these data do not support confident interpretation of those edges. The plot presents the edge estimates alongside their intervals, ordered by weight:

plot(b)

How precise is each node’s centrality?

The bootstrap samples also provide intervals for node centrality. Strength is the sum of the absolute weights of a node’s edges, whereas expected influence sums signed edge weights. This distinction matters when the network contains both positive and negative associations.

as.data.frame(b, what = "centrality")
#>   node  strength strength_lower strength_upper expected_influence
#> 1  CSU 1.4794795      1.3523996       1.667857          1.4794795
#> 2   IV 0.9920086      0.8349704       1.266730          0.1598207
#> 3   SE 1.2652845      1.0903270       1.502809         -0.3743445
#> 4   SR 1.9520259      1.8288036       2.030832          1.0956629
#> 5   TA 1.3851959      1.2491191       1.574835         -0.3340278
#>   expected_influence_lower expected_influence_upper
#> 1               1.35239959                1.6678566
#> 2               0.01245256                0.2507549
#> 3              -0.45804609               -0.2573138
#> 4               0.96124498                1.2166942
#> 5              -0.43162878               -0.2568683
plot(b, type = "centrality")

Self-regulation (SR) has the highest observed strength, 1.95, with a bootstrap interval from 1.83 to 2.03. This interval does not overlap the interval of any other node. Intrinsic value (IV) has the lowest observed strength, 0.99, with an interval from 0.83 to 1.27. The intervals for cognitive strategy use, self-efficacy and test anxiety overlap, so their ranking cannot be inferred from separate intervals alone. Expected influence answers a different question: self-efficacy and test anxiety have negative values (-0.37 and -0.33), reflecting the balance of their signed edges. The next analysis compares strengths directly.

Which nodes can be ranked?

difference_test() compares the centralities of pairs of nodes or the weights of pairs of edges. It calculates each difference across the existing bootstrap samples, then reports its percentile interval and a two-sided bootstrap p-value. The stored samples from net_boot() are reused rather than fitted again. For the ten pairwise strength comparisons, p_adjust = "BH" applies a false discovery rate adjustment to the p-values (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995). An interval containing zero indicates that the bootstrap differences do not clearly distinguish the pair.

difference_test(b, type = "strength", p_adjust = "BH")
#>    item1 item2    value1    value2    obs_diff        lower       upper
#> 1    CSU    IV 1.4794795 0.9920086  0.48747089  0.241546367  0.66372411
#> 2    CSU    SE 1.4794795 1.2652845  0.21419501  0.038286544  0.42634973
#> 3     IV    SE 0.9920086 1.2652845 -0.27327588 -0.334413124 -0.13532664
#> 4    CSU    SR 1.4794795 1.9520259 -0.47254639 -0.623609013 -0.21321640
#> 5     IV    SR 0.9920086 1.9520259 -0.96001728 -1.093928157 -0.59055176
#> 6     SE    SR 1.2652845 1.9520259 -0.68674140 -0.877109385 -0.38029431
#> 7    CSU    TA 1.4794795 1.3851959  0.09428358  0.003900685  0.19887099
#> 8     IV    TA 0.9920086 1.3851959 -0.39318731 -0.563676398 -0.15302913
#> 9     SE    TA 1.2652845 1.3851959 -0.11991143 -0.332646886  0.08003091
#> 10    SR    TA 1.9520259 1.3851959  0.56682997  0.285722615  0.69319578
#>       p_value significant
#> 1  0.00000000        TRUE
#> 2  0.04444444        TRUE
#> 3  0.00000000        TRUE
#> 4  0.00000000        TRUE
#> 5  0.00000000        TRUE
#> 6  0.00000000        TRUE
#> 7  0.04444444        TRUE
#> 8  0.00000000        TRUE
#> 9  0.26000000       FALSE
#> 10 0.00000000        TRUE

Nine of the ten comparisons have intervals excluding zero and are flagged as significant in the output. Self-regulation has greater strength than every other node, with adjusted p-values reported as 0 for these comparisons at the available bootstrap resolution. Cognitive strategy use also exceeds self-efficacy and test anxiety (adjusted p = 0.044 for each comparison). The only pair not distinguished is self-efficacy and test anxiety: their observed difference is -0.12, with an interval from -0.33 to 0.08 and an adjusted p-value of 0.26. Thus, self-regulation can be placed first and intrinsic value last in this example, but the evidence does not establish an ordering between self-efficacy and test anxiety.

Is the centrality ranking stable when cases are dropped?

net_stability() re-estimates the network on random subsets that drop an increasing proportion of the respondents and correlates the centralities of each subset with those of the full sample. The correlation-stability coefficient (CS-coefficient) is the largest proportion of cases that can be dropped while the correlation stays at or above 0.7 in at least 95% of the subsets (Epskamp et al., 2018).

st <- net_stability(SRL_Claude, method = "glasso", iter = 100)
st
#> <psychnet_stability> glasso, 100 subsets/proportion
#>   CS-coefficient (pearson cor > 0.70 in > 95% of subsets):
#>     strength             0.70
#>     expected_influence   0.90

The reported CS-coefficients are 0.70 for strength and 0.90 for expected influence. Under the diagnostic’s criterion, a drop proportion of 0.70 retains correlations of at least 0.7 with full-sample strength in at least 95% of the sampled subsets. Epskamp et al. (2018) recommend a coefficient above 0.25, preferably above 0.5, for interpreting centrality. Both estimates comfortably exceed these reference values. This supports the stability of the centrality pattern in the example, although it does not resolve every pairwise difference. The plot displays mean correlations by drop proportion, with a band showing one standard deviation and a horizontal threshold at 0.7:

plot(st)

Is the edge structure stable when cases are dropped?

net_casedrop_reliability() applies the same case-dropping design to the edges. At each drop proportion it compares the edge weights of each subset with those of the full sample through their correlation and through the mean, median and largest absolute difference. The edge-weight CS-coefficient is defined as for centrality.

cd <- net_casedrop_reliability(SRL_Claude, method = "glasso", iter = 100)
cd
#> # edge-weight stability: glasso | CS = 0.90 (pearson cor > 0.70 in > 95% of subsets)

The edge-weight CS-coefficient is 0.90. Mean correlations between subset and full-sample edge weights are 0.999 after dropping 10% of cases and 0.943 after dropping 90%, suggesting that the overall arrangement of edge weights is retained across the sampled subsets. This does not mean that individual estimates remain equally precise. The mean absolute deviation rises from 0.012 to 0.112 across these drop proportions, while the mean maximum absolute deviation rises from 0.028 to 0.261. At the largest drop proportion, appreciable differences in individual edge estimates can therefore coexist with a high overall correlation.

plot(cd)

Does the network replicate across halves of the sample?

net_split_reliability() divides the sample at random into two halves, estimates a network on each, and compares the two sets of edges, repeating the split many times. The result has one row per comparison measure, with its mean, standard deviation and the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles across splits.

rel <- net_split_reliability(SRL_Claude, method = "glasso", iter = 100)
rel
#> # split-half reliability: glasso | 100 iterations (50/50 split)
#>           metric       mean         sd      lower     upper n_valid
#> 1   mean_abs_dev 0.06406132 0.02201012 0.03319670 0.1092927     100
#> 2 median_abs_dev 0.05674286 0.02297601 0.02204948 0.1086049     100
#> 3    correlation 0.98243129 0.01208858 0.95313106 0.9960735     100
#> 4    max_abs_dev 0.14177087 0.05219793 0.06749545 0.2635560     100

Across 100 random 50/50 splits, the mean correlation between the two sets of edge weights is 0.982. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the correlations are 0.953 and 0.996. Each half contains 150 observations, but the halves are repeatedly drawn from the same dataset, not from two new independent studies. The mean absolute edge-weight deviation across splits is 0.064, and the mean of the maximum absolute deviations is 0.142. These results indicate strong agreement in the overall edge pattern within this dataset, alongside some variation in particular edge weights; they do not by themselves demonstrate external replication.

plot(rel)

Do the diagnostics apply to other estimators?

Each diagnostic refits the network through psychnet(method = ), so it applies to any estimator. With the unregularized partial correlation network:

net_casedrop_reliability(SRL_Claude, method = "pcor", iter = 100)

The unregularised partial correlation network also has an edge-weight CS-coefficient of 0.90. Its mean absolute deviations exceed those of the graphical lasso at each reported drop proportion, reaching 0.139 rather than 0.112 when 90% of cases are dropped. The absence of regularisation may contribute to this difference, but these figures alone do not establish its cause. Each diagnostic also accepts group networks fitted using psychnet(..., group = ) and returns results for each group.

When to use which diagnostic

Question Verb Read the result with
How precise is each edge and centrality? net_boot() as.data.frame(b), as.data.frame(b, what = "centrality"), plot()
Do two edges or two nodes differ? difference_test() the returned table, plot()
Is the centrality order stable when cases are dropped? net_stability() as.data.frame(st, what = "cs"), as.data.frame(st), plot()
Is the edge structure stable when cases are dropped? net_casedrop_reliability() the returned table, plot()
Does the network replicate across halves? net_split_reliability() the returned table, plot()
  • Report bootstrap intervals for edges of substantive interest. Treat an interval containing zero as insufficient evidence to interpret that edge confidently, rather than as proof that the relationship is absent.
  • Use pairwise difference tests alongside case-dropping stability when discussing node rankings. A CS-coefficient below 0.25 warrants particular caution about centrality interpretation.
  • Distinguish uncertainty in a particular edge from agreement in the network as a whole. Here, high case-dropping and split-half correlations coexist with two edge intervals that include zero.
  • These procedures assume independent observations. For repeated observations from the same individuals, resampling must respect the dependence between observations from each individual.
